text: On 16 September 2021, Lauren Anne Dickason, a South African immigrant, murdered her three daughters—6-year-old Liané and 2-year-old twins Maya and Karla—at her home in Timaru, New Zealand. After admitting to the killings, she denied murder and instead pleaded insanity or infanticide. She was found guilty of murdering her three children on 16 August 2023 and sentenced on 26 June 2024 to 18 years in prison, with no minimum term and will remain in a mental health hospital until deemed mentally fit for prison. Dickason is the daughter of Malcolm and Wendy Fawkes. She attended a boarding school in Pretoria, South Africa, and from age 15 experienced depression and anxiety, along with post-natal depression. She studied medicine at the University of Cape Town, graduating in 2004, and completed rural health practice in Pretoria, where she met her husband Graham Dickason, an orthopaedic surgeon, in 2005. They married in 2006. Dickason faced multiple fertility issues, undergoing 17 rounds of IVF and using donor eggs; she had her first child, Sarah, in 2013, who died shortly after birth, prompting her to stop working and become a part-time surgeon assistant to Graham. She later had three more children: Liané, born in September 2014, and twins Maya and Karla, born in November 2018. Following the twins' birth, the family hired a nanny, Maria Mendy Sibanyoni, who worked from November 2018 to May 2020. Dickason was diagnosed in 2015 with "major depression with underlying anxiety," linked to postpartum depression following Sarah’s death, and experienced flashbacks, sleep difficulties, crying, suicidal thoughts, panic attacks, restlessness, detachment, and intrusive thoughts. Anxiety and depression also affected her during and after the birth of the twins, due to Karla’s cleft palate. In May 2019, after struggling to put her twins to bed, she saw a psychiatrist and reported homicidal thoughts, citing Karla’s frequent outbursts, including slapping and biting, and stating her children were "never enough." The family planned to emigrate to New Zealand in August 2020 but faced delays due to the global COVID-19 pandemic and immigration issues. Though she experienced depression and suicidal thoughts during the pandemic, her mood improved between late 2020 and June 2021, with the Crown claiming a remission lasting at least two months. Dickason stopped taking her antidepressants in March 2021 without consulting her doctor but resumed them in August 2021. Her mental health worsened in July 2021 during South African unrest following Jacob Zuma’s imprisonment, leading her to fear for her children’s safety and have thoughts of harming them; she confided in Graham, who convinced her to restart medication. She continued to have homicidal thoughts after a foot surgery but did not disclose them due to concerns about immigration plans. In July 2021, a friend sent her a TikTok video titled "Mom needs a minute," which she responded to by saying "Awesome xxx, that's exactly how I feel." Over the following months, she searched online for methods to overdose her children. In August 2021, after seeing her husband and daughters play with cable ties in the garage, she had thoughts of using them to asphyxiate her children, two weeks before the family moved to New Zealand. She became withdrawn, cried frequently, and her mother Wendy noted significant weight loss. The family arrived in Timaru on 11 September 2021, five days before the killings, and Dickason was unhappy with the town, describing it as "small, disgusting and creepy," fearing cyberbullying for her children and comparing New Zealand’s treatment of Māori to apartheid in South Africa. Defence experts stated these concerns became delusions reinforced by her depression. The children were murdered on the night of 16 September 2021. On that day, Karla and Maya attended their first day at preschool and Liané attended her second day at Timaru Christian School. After picking up her daughters, Karla threw a tantrum in the car. The family visited the local botanical gardens, where Dickason believed a group of girls warned her that a boy was photographing her children, leading her to believe New Zealand was as dangerous as South Africa. That day, she had thoughts of "brutally killing" the children by sedating them and cutting their femoral arteries. Graham went out with colleagues, leaving Lauren alone with the children. During a police interview, she told detectives the children were "being wild again, jumping on the couches, not listening to what I'm trying to tell them" and that "something just triggered me." She later told investigators that the trigger was an Immigration NZ request for medical information about Karla’s cleft palate and her own mental health, and her feeling she couldn’t make the children’s school lunches. After gathering the children in a bedroom, she told them they were making necklaces with cable ties and tricked them into wearing the ties around their necks, telling them "Mummy's very sick and is going to die. I can't leave you behind because I don't know who’s going to look after you." She then asphyxiated the children, starting with Karla, then Liané and Maya. She told police that Karla had been "really horrible" and that Liané had fought back, recalling that the oldest child was angry and asked why she was doing this, saying she loved her and was the best mum. Since the children were still breathing, she smothered them with a towel and their blankets. Afterwards, she attempted suicide with a knife and pills. The bodies were discovered in their beds by Graham upon returning home. He confronted a distraught Dickason, who told him it was "too late" before falling into a catatonic state. At 10 pm on 16 September 2021, police responded to a call from neighbours Karen and Brad Cowper, who found Graham distraught. At the house, police found the three dead children and Lauren Dickason, who was hospitalised in stable condition. Graham’s colleague Mark Cvitanich and his wife Cathy also responded to Graham’s phone call and called police and emergency services. Dickason was taken to Timaru Hospital. On 17 September, police interviewed Dickason, who admitted to killing her three children. Detective Inspector Scott Anderson confirmed the arrest of a 40-year-old woman in connection with the deaths and stated the incident was isolated and no one else was being sought. On 18 September, Dickason appeared in the Timaru District Court and was remanded to a forensic psychiatric ward at Christchurch’s Hillmorton Hospital, later placed in a hospital psychiatric unit. At Hillmorton, she was interviewed by five forensic psychiatrists and psychologists for 53 hours. Three—Susan Hatters-Friedman, Justin Barry-Walsh, and Ghazi Metoui—believed she was severely mentally unwell and could claim a defence of insanity or infanticide. The other two, Erik Monasterio and Simone McLeavey, believed she killed her children out of anger and control, including not wanting another woman to parent them if she died or Graham remarried. On 5 October 2021, her lawyer Kerryn Beaton QC sought an extended remand, delaying her court appearance due to a mental health assessment. On 15 October, Beaton told the Christchurch court that Dickason would plead not guilty to three charges of murder. She was unable to attend due to illness and sought further remand, which was not opposed by Crown prosecutor Andrew McRae. A trial date for March 2023 was set. The trial began on 17 July 2023 at the Christchurch High Court, presided over by Judge Cameron Mander and with Andrew McRae as Crown prosecutor. McRae detailed the circumstances of the deaths and Dickason’s attempted suicide, while defence lawyer Anne Toohey outlined the defence’s arguments. The Crown argued Dickason murdered her children due to resentment over their impact on her marriage, while Dickason denied murder due to insanity or infanticide. Testimony included Graham, emergency responders, and the children’s teachers, along with digital forensic evidence and Dickason’s police interview. On 26 July, the Crown rested its case. Defence counsel Toohey argued that Dickason’s decision to kill her children was "spontaneous" because she believed her and the children’s lives were not worth living and that they were "all better off dead." The defence relied on expert witnesses: Dr Susan Hatters-Friedman, Dr Justin Barry-Walsh, and Dr Ghazi Metoui. The prosecution called Dr Erik Monasterio and Dr Simone McLeavey. On 11 August, McRae delivered his closing address, stating Dickason knew her actions were morally wrong and that the key drivers were "anger and control." He emphasized that the trial was by jury, not experts, and that defence experts had not assessed her at the time of the killing, while the Crown had. The Crown argued defence experts ignored crucial information and that Dickason’s accounts were inconsistent. It claimed postpartum depression had remitted and was at best a minimal contributor. The Crown said the defence experts’ evidence should be treated with caution, noting Dickason reported killing Karla first due to her misbehaviour, such as biting and scratching. The defence countered that Karla was killed first because she was closest to Dickason. When asked if postpartum depression caused the killings, Dickason said "no," and that the idea "just popped up," though the Crown later stated the thoughts did not just appear. The defence’s closing address, starting at 2:30 pm, mentioned her 16 rounds of IVF, the family’s move to New Zealand to provide a better life for the children, the world being dangerous for them, postpartum depression after the twins’ birth, her severe mental illness, her husband’s lack of understanding, her reliability and consistency with experts, that she was not asked by police why she killed them, and that she did not tell anyone she killed them out of anger. The defence also noted her brother, sister, or close family could have provided context. On the fifth week, Justice Mander summed up the case, discussing the police interview the day after the deaths and instructing the jury not to let emotion—such as sympathy or media-driven prejudice—alter their judgment. He noted there was no dispute that Dickason caused the deaths, and the issue was whether it was murder, infanticide, or insanity due to an undisputed mental imbalance. He summarised the expert evidence. On 16 August 2023, Dickason was found guilty of three counts of murder after 15 hours of deliberation, with a 11-1 majority verdict rejecting infanticide and insanity defences and accepting the Crown’s argument that she acted "methodically, purposefully and even clinically out of anger and control." Dickason stood motionless as the verdict was delivered and wept as she was led out. Both her lawyers and several jurors wept. Justice Mander remanded her to Hillmorton Hospital under a compulsory treatment order, stating prison was inappropriate and requested expert reports on her mental state and an appropriate sentence. Her parents, Malcolm and Wendy Fawkes, issued a statement blaming postpartum depression for the deaths of their grandchildren and urged greater awareness of its effects. The judge sought to determine the sentence length and type following a mental health assessment. The Sentencing Act presumes life imprisonment for murder unless it would be "manifestly unjust." The decision on whether Dickason would serve time in prison or remain in a psychiatric unit has not yet been made. She will not be extradited to South Africa. In early September 2023, her sentencing date was set for 19 December 2023, later postponed to 2024, then to 20 March, and finally rescheduled to 26 June due to delays in determining her placement. Until then, she remained at Hillmorton Hospital. On 26 June 2024, she was sentenced to 18 years in prison as three concurrent determinate sentences, with no minimum term and will remain in a mental health hospital until deemed mentally fit. During sentencing, victim impact statements from family members, including Graham and both paternal and maternal relatives, were read. Dickason has been served with a deportation order that will take effect upon her release. In early August 2024, her legal team lodged an appeal against the conviction in the New Zealand Court of Appeal on 23 July; the grounds have not been disclosed. If successful, a second trial could occur. The New Zealand government granted $709,000 for Dickason’s defence, including $153,970 for three psychiatric or psychological reports and $71,062.50 for other expenses.

On 26 June 2024, Lauren Dickason was sentenced to 18 years in prison, consisting of three concurrent determinate sentences of 18 years, with no minimum term of imprisonment. She will remain in Hillmorton Hospital until deemed mentally fit for prison. During the sentencing, she remained silent and showed no reaction, and victim impact statements from her family members, including Graham and both paternal and maternal relatives, were read. A deportation order has been served against her, which will take effect upon her release from prison. On 23 July 2024, her legal team lodged an appeal in the New Zealand Court of Appeal, though the grounds have not been disclosed; if successful, a second trial could occur. The New Zealand government provided $709,000 for her defence, including $153,970 for three psychiatric or psychological reports, $71,062.50 for a forensic psychologist, $58,700.81 for expert witnesses, $39,945.78 for other witness disbursements, $6,367.50 for a private investigator, $9,480 for computer forensics, and $3,000 for expert legal opinion. Her legal team spent 1714.25 hours on the defence, with Crown Solicitor Andrew McRae spending 732.5 hours. On 18 September 2021, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) assisted the Dickason family's relatives in traveling to New Zealand and securing managed isolation under COVID-19 quarantine rules. The former nanny Mari Sibanyoni expressed shock and grief upon learning of the children's deaths. On 23 September 2021, a candelight vigil was held in Timaru’s Queen Street in honour of Lianne, Maya, and Karla Dickason, during which Graham read a letter expressing forgiveness for his wife and thanking friends and family, and a similar service was held in Pretoria; Graham returned to South Africa in December 2021. Neighbours Rob and Jade Whaley built a memorial garden in Timaru, including an "Angel Dickason tree" with three white stones in memory of the girls. The Independent Online’s Jehran Naidoo compared Dickason to American mother Andrea Yates, noting both suffered from mental illness and post-partum depression, had experienced previous miscarriages, had professionally-accomplished husbands, and killed their children while their husbands were away. In mid-August 2023, Timaru Mayor Nigel Bowen welcomed the jury’s guilty verdict, stating it ended a dark period for the town and urged community members to check on one another, emphasizing that mental health was still stigmatized. Judge Mander, Detective Inspector Scott Anderson, chaplain Alan Cummings, and South Canterbury Chief Medical Officer Dr Ben Pearson all extended sympathies to the victims’ families and welcomed the verdict as closure. Current affairs bloggers David Farrar and Martyn "Bomber" Bradbury described the verdict as justice for the deceased children. Following her conviction, supporters established a Facebook group called "Support for Lauren Dickason" in July 2022, which grew to over 1,900 members from multiple countries, mostly women, with the spokesperson stating the verdict had silenced women’s voices. The group planned a march and picnic in Christchurch in November 2023, walking from the justice precinct to the Botanic Gardens with "support not silence" T-shirts and sunflowers, and holding a picnic in support of maternal mental health. Supporter Tanya Parker organized a petition urging Judge Mander to consider postpartum depression in sentencing and for the legal profession to recognize it as a public health crisis. The group also produced a 370-page book of supportive letters titled 'Lauren: Our love and support,' which was sent to Dickason on the second anniversary of the children’s deaths. In early October, The Press reported that Dickason wrote a letter to her supporters thanking them for their love during a difficult time, revealing she had made three teddy bears from her daughters’ clothing and stated she could never forgive herself for what happened. In response to media attention, Hillmorton Hospital restricted her communications, banning letters during the sentencing period, though these restrictions were later lifted, allowing her to receive letters again.
